tagline.text: A colorful Chinese Taoist temple at the gateway to Baguio

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Balili, La Trinidad, Benguet, near the Baguio city boundary (on Halsema Highway)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~300 (per person, covering entrance fee, transport and snacks)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Bell Church is a Chinese temple at the entrance of La Trinidad, just north of Baguio, with a dragon-decorated gate, octagonal ponds, pagodas and gardens. It is only about 10 minutes from downtown by jeepney, so it makes an easy short stop on a Baguio trip.

Bell Church is a Chinese temple in Barangay Balili, La Trinidad, Benguet. Despite the name, it is not a Christian church but a temple with Taoist and Buddhist character, built by a Chinese immigrant community and located very close to the Baguio city boundary. According to Wikipedia, the grounds cover about 10,000 square meters and lie near the 3-kilometer mark of Halsema Highway. It sits on the road leading from Baguio toward the La Trinidad strawberry farms and the Benguet highlands, so it fits easily into an itinerary. The temple lies in a lower part of the valley than downtown Baguio, and you can notice the scenery change on the way down from the city.

Its history goes back to the 1960s. Per Wikipedia, it was founded on August 4, 1960, by Taishanese and Cantonese Chinese immigrants centered on Ng Pee, when the area still belonged to Mountain Province. Ng Pee is said to have begun preaching in a restaurant hall around 1954 and, as the congregation grew, moved the gatherings to his home at the 6-kilometer mark before building the temple on its present site. It was first called the "Chinese Buddhist Temple," but the name Bell Church gradually took hold. The site is said to have been chosen for its good feng shui. In 1970 it was reportedly recognized as a major tourist destination by then Tourism Secretary Jose Aspiras, and it was often used as a filming location for Philippine films from the 1970s to the 1990s.

What makes the temple distinctive is a faith that embraces five religions. Wikipedia explains that it venerates five patron saints representing Taoism, Confucianism, Islam, Christianity and Buddhism. Devotees consult the saints through a spiritual medium, asking about business, marriage and personal worries. Visitors do not need to take part in this practice, but for that reason the place is known locally as somewhere people come to seek guidance or peace of mind. Cultural events of the Filipino-Chinese community, as well as lion dance, dragon dance and martial arts classes, continue in the gymnasium here.

This guide is for travelers staying in Baguio who want a half-day trip outside the city center. The site is not large, and about 30 minutes is enough even at a relaxed pace. Combining it with the colorful hillside houses of the nearby Valley of Colors makes an efficient pair of stops on a single trip. Entrance fees and opening hours vary slightly between sources, so check the latest information before you go. If you want to learn more about the temple's story and faith, read the notices on site slowly. Even a short visit gives a glimpse of another side of Baguio, the history of the Chinese community in the Philippines.
The colorful arch at the entrance has dragon sculptures and Chinese inscriptions. Its red and gold stand out, and it is the spot where most visitors take photos.

In front of the main hall are two octagonal (bagua) ponds planted with lotuses. The octagon stands for rebirth and immortality, and the lotus for purity and beauty. Do not sit or stand on the edge of the ponds.
Several pagodas house images of saints and the Buddha. The grounds also hold a bust of the founder, Ng Pee, which helps you picture how the temple began.
The grounds are said to include a statue of Guan Gong, a figure who symbolizes trust in business and goodness. He is a common object of devotion in Chinese temples, so it is interesting to compare.

Walking along the Asian-style garden, you reach the upper part, where you can see toward Baguio and the Quirino Hill area. The climb is short, so older travelers and children can manage it without trouble.

The gymnasium on the grounds hosts dragon dance, lion dance and martial arts classes. If a class is in session you can watch from a distance, and special performances are sometimes held at Lunar New Year.

The bell that gives the temple its name is used mainly in religious rituals and is said to have once warned of disasters. Inside the main hall you can see the altar and incense rituals. The mix of incense smoke and the sound of the bell is a completely different experience from the churches of downtown Baguio.

items.title: Short half-day route
items.subtitle: Bell Church and the Valley of Colors

children.text: Take a jeepney bound for La Trinidad from the Burnham Park area in Baguio and get off near the Bell Church entrance. If you arrive before the crowds come in, before
, you will have room to take photos.
Pay the entrance fee at the front gate and look around the dragon gate, octagonal ponds and pagodas in turn. Be careful not to step onto the pond edges.
Inside the main hall, do not take photos or video, take off your hat and look around quietly. If worshippers are offering incense, keep your distance so you do not disturb them.
Climb to the viewpoint at the top of the garden, take in the view toward Baguio and head back down.
Walk about
10 minutes
to the Valley of Colors and photograph the colorful houses on the hillside.
Head toward La Trinidad town for lunch, or continue to a strawberry farm to end the day.
Count on about 30 minutes to 1 hour at Bell Church, not including travel time. The temple faces Halsema Highway, which is busy, so be careful on the shoulder and when crossing if you walk.

items.title: A full day linked with Baguio
items.subtitle: Baguio and La Trinidad in one trip

children.text: Have breakfast at your hotel in Baguio and head to the jeepney stop near Burnham Park.
Take a La Trinidad jeepney to Bell Church and spend about an hour looking around the grounds.
Walk to the Valley of Colors, enjoy the view of the hillside village and take photos.
Move toward La Trinidad town, stopping at a strawberry farm or the local market, and have lunch.
Return to Baguio and spend the afternoon relaxing around Session Road or Burnham Park.
Strawberry farm operating conditions change with the season, so check before you visit.
Take a long-distance bus from Manila to Baguio city. Depending on traffic it takes about
5–6 hours
. Check the bus company's announcements for exact fares and departure terminals.
By private car or rental car, the usual route goes via NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX up to Baguio, and takes around
4 hours
depending on road conditions.
After reaching Baguio, use the local transport options below to get to Bell Church.
Getting from Manila to Baguio overland is the usual choice. Check airline and bus company announcements for the latest operating information.
Board a La Trinidad-bound jeepney at the stop near Burnham Park in Baguio. The fare is roughly
. As of April 2026 the official fare is ₱13, but some drivers charge around ₱20 because of higher fuel costs, so check when you board.
Tell the driver you are getting off at "Bell Church" and he will stop near the entrance. The front gate is a few steps away.
Depending on road conditions it takes about
10–30 minutes
A taxi from downtown Baguio takes around
20 minutes
, and the fare is known to be around
. Check whether the meter is used.
On the way back you can flag down a jeepney on the road in front of the temple.

Much of Bell Church is outdoors, so the weather matters. The Baguio area is high in elevation and cool all year, but when it rains the stone paving on the grounds gets slippery and walking in the garden is less pleasant.

During the Lunar New Year holidays, lion and dragon dance performances are held, and you can see worshippers offering coins and food, it is said. The trade-off is heavy crowds, so for a quiet visit early on a weekday is better.

According to Wikipedia, the temple also observes the Hungry Ghost Festival (Poh Toh), which falls in the seventh lunar month. The exact dates and schedule change every year, so if your trip overlaps, it is best to check with the temple.

rows: Pleasant for walking, like early autumn in Korea. The year-end peak season is crowded throughout Baguio
Dry season, strong sun by day

Bell Church itself has no lodging, so most travelers stay in downtown Baguio and visit as a half-day trip. Around Burnham Park and near Session Road there is a wide choice of hotels, guesthouses and Korean-run guesthouses, which makes getting around easy.

For meals you can eat something simple near the temple or move on to La Trinidad town. Baguio has many Korean restaurants, so if you miss Korean food you can return downtown to eat. Restaurant names in this area change often, so check recent reviews.

La Trinidad is famous for Benguet highland vegetables and strawberries, so in season you will notice stalls selling strawberry snacks and fresh vegetables. A cold drink after the temple visit is a nice way to take a break.
Arriving before
, when more visitors start to come, makes taking photos much easier.
Photos and videos are said not to be allowed inside the main hall, so read the notice at the entrance first.
It is polite to remove your cap or bonnet once you enter the grounds.
Do not sit or stand on the edge of the octagonal ponds. They are structures with religious meaning.
Bell Church and the Valley of Colors are about
10 minutes
apart on foot, so combine them in one trip.
Hours are known to be roughly 7:00 to 17:00, but some sources list a midday break (12:00-13:30) and a 16:00 closing, so check the latest information before visiting. Entrance is free or around ₱20.
When taking a jeepney, have small change ready and tell the driver in advance where you will get off.
Because it is a place of worship, it is safer to avoid short shorts and very revealing clothes.
If you are interested in the temple's founding and its oracle culture, reading an introduction such as Wikipedia beforehand makes the visit much more enjoyable.
This is a place of worship, so behave quietly and do not photograph worshippers' prayers or rituals without permission.
Entrance fees and hours differ between sources and need to be confirmed locally.
The road in front of the temple is Halsema Highway with heavy traffic, so be careful on the shoulder and when crossing if you walk.
The stone steps and paving on the grounds can be slippery on rainy days.
It gets very crowded on weekends and at Lunar New Year, so watch your belongings.
Fortune-telling and the medium's rituals are optional. If you are asked for payment, confirm the amount first.
A hillside mural village about
10 minutes
away on foot. It is right next to the La Trinidad welcome arch, so it is easy to find.
A place where you can pick Benguet's specialty strawberries yourself. It lies in the same direction as Bell Church, so it is easy to visit next.
A lake park in the center of Baguio. It is a convenient starting point for taking a jeepney.
From Bell Church to the city center is about
20 minutes
by car. It is a good base to stay in and fit into your itinerary.
